text: Some data is naturally hierarchical — an org chart, a folder structure, or, right here in AdventureWorks2012, a bill of materials. A bicycle is assembled from components, and some of those components are themselves assemblies made of further components. A regular query can't walk an arbitrary number of levels — you'd have to already know how deep it goes. That's exactly what a recursive CTE solves.

A recursive CTE has two parts, joined by UNION ALL. The anchor member, before UNION ALL, is the starting point — here, the top-level assembly's direct components, at level zero. The recursive member, after UNION ALL, references BOMHierarchy by its own name — and that self-reference is exactly what makes this recursive. Each pass finds the next level down, joining components-of-components onto whatever the previous pass found, incrementing the level each time.

And here's the part that feels almost magical the first time you see it: SQL Server just keeps repeating that recursive member, automatically, until a pass produces no new rows at all. That's how it walks a hierarchy of completely unknown depth without you ever specifying how many levels to check.

One hard requirement, not a style choice: recursive CTEs must use UNION ALL, never plain UNION. UNION's deduplication from Lesson 38 isn't just unnecessary here — T-SQL's recursive CTE syntax actually disallows it outright.

Anchor to start, recursive member to reach the next level, UNION ALL required, and it stops itself once nothing new turns up. Next lesson: VIEW, a genuinely saved, reusable version of everything a CTE almost is. See you there.
